ABSTRACT This observational study investigated the potential influence of hormonal contraceptive (HC) use on selected hormonal biomarkers (estradiol, total testosterone, IGF‐1, cortisol, triiodothyronine, and leptin) that respond to diet and physical training–induced low energy availability (LEA). Thirty‐six female physique athletes—combined HC users ( n = 11), low‐dose progestin‐only HC users ( n = 11), and naturally menstruating females ( n = 14)—prepared for a physique competition. All participants voluntarily restricted energy intake while simultaneously participating in resistance training to maintain lean mass and aerobic training to increase energy expenditure. Measurements were completed over approximately 46 weeks as follows: before commencing the pre‐competition period, including dietary restriction and physical training (pre); after ∼23 weeks of dietary restriction and physical training (post); and after ∼23 weeks of recovery (recovery). Hormones were analyzed from fasting blood samples, whereas body mass, fat mass, fat‐free mass, and body fat percentage were measured using bioimpedance. Our main findings established that after ∼23 weeks of LEA, concentrations of estradiol and total testosterone remained stable in the combined HC users but decreased significantly in progestin‐only HC users and naturally menstruating females. Serum IGF‐1, triiodothyronine, and leptin decreased comparably from pre to post in all groups, whereas serum cortisol concentrations remained statistically unchanged throughout the investigation. These results indicate that the exogenous hormones in combined HCs users may maintain already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis function in the presence of LEA, whereas LEA‐induced changes in IGF‐1, triiodothyronine, and leptin may be comparable in combined and progestin‐only HC users and naturally menstruating females. Trial Registration The second study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT04392752 Highlights Combined hormonal contraceptive users maintain already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis function in the presence of low energy availability (maintained estradiol and total testosterone concentrations), but hormonal contraceptive users and naturally menstruating females experience comparable, potentially negative, and endocrine consequences of low energy availability including significant decreases in concentrations of IGF‐1, triiodothyronine, and leptin. Hormonal contraceptive users and physicians prescribing hormonal contraceptives should be made aware that diet and physical training–induced low energy availability might negatively affect endocrine health. Roughly 50% of elite female athletes use HCs, where combined oral HCs are currently the most common (up to 70% of HC users) (Martin et al. 2018 ) and the use of hormonal (progestin‐only) intrauterine devices (IUDs) is increasing (Ekenros et al. 2022 ) although its prevalence is country‐dependent (Lindh et al. 2017 ; United Nations 2019 ). Combined HCs are composed of an estrogen (synthetic ethinyl estradiol) and a progestin (synthetic progesterone), where progestin‐only HCs contain only progestin. Combined HCs suppress hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) function, resulting in decreased pituitary gonadotropin secretion and lower concentrations of endogenous female sex steroids such as estradiol (E2) and progesterone (Rivera et al. 1999 ). Progestin‐only HCs may suppress HPO axis function in higher exogenous doses (Teal and Edelman 2021 ) whereas lower exogenous doses such as those delivered by minipills and hormonal IUDs do not suppress HPO axis function or do so inconsistently (Spencer et al. 2009 ; Grimes et al. 2013 ). As such, the endogenous sex steroid profile in low‐dose progestin‐only users may closely mimic that of naturally menstruating/eumenorrheic individuals (Spencer et al. 2009 ; Grimes et al. 2013 ). While the primary purpose of combined HCs is to suppress female sex steroid production, combined HCs also tend to decrease circulating concentrations of total and free testosterone with a concomitant increase in sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) concentrations (Zimmerman et al. 2014 ). Combined HCs also tend to influence the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis resulting in higher total cortisol concentrations in combined HC users than nonusers (Hertel et al. 2017 ; Masama et al. 2022 ) although this observation is inconsistent (Kirschbaum et al. 1996 ; Larsen et al. 2020 ). An increase in growth hormone (GH) concentrations via estrogen's effect on the pituitary gland, concomitant with a decrease in insulin‐like growth factor 1 (IGF‐1), may be also observed in combined HC users (Southmayd and De Souza 2017 ; Birzniece and Ho 2021 ). The decrease in IGF‐1 may be due to estrogen's direct inhibitory effect on IGF‐1 synthesis in the liver or altered GH signaling; however, there does not appear to be significant differences in GH or IGF‐1 concentrations between naturally menstruating females and combined HC users (Massa et al. 1993 ; Riechman and Lee 2022 ; Özcan et al. 2024 ). Combined HCs, such as those containing, for example, dienogest and levonorgestrel, may increase thyroid hormones [total triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4)] due to an increase in binding to serum globulins, but the free fractions of these hormones appear to be only slightly changed or unchanged (Torre et al. 2020 ). The systemic effects of progestin‐only HCs have not been as widely investigated, although it has been suggested that progestin‐only HCs only have a minor effect on systemic metabolism and inflammation (Wang et al. 2016 ). Indeed, progestin‐only pills containing desogestrel or levonorgestrel do not appear to significantly affect thyroid function (Kivelä et al. 2001 ). Low energy availability (LEA), an energy availability (EA) of < 30 kcal·kg −1 FFM·day −1 ], refers to a mismatch between dietary energy intakes (EI) to cover the energy cost of exercise (exercise energy expenditure, EEE), which results in suboptimal energy for physiological processes in the body, including those related to the maintenance of health and supporting training adaptations in athletes (Loucks et al. 2011 ). The equation EA = (EI−EEE)/FFM (where FFM = fat‐free mass) is often used to estimate EA, although protocols for evaluating EI, EEE, and FFM have not universally been agreed upon thus leaving some room for error (Burke et al. 2018 ). The effects of LEA, which may be induced by, for example, diet and physical training, on endocrine function have been reported in several publications (Elliott‐Sale et al. 2018 ; Ackerman and Misra 2018 ; Dipla et al. 2020 ; Areta et al. 2020 ; Ihalainen et al. 2024 ). For example, LEA has been reported to decrease gonadotropin‐releasing hormone resulting in downstream suppression of luteinizing hormone, estrogen, and testosterone whereas a decrease in thyroid hormones (e.g., T3), leptin, IGF‐1, and insulin and an increase in cortisol, growth hormone, and ghrelin have been reported (Elliott‐Sale et al. 2018 ; Ackerman and Misra 2018 ; Dipla et al. 2020 ; Areta et al. 2020 ; Ihalainen et al. 2024 ). Much of this research has focused on menstrual dysfunction and bone health, as well as the identification of surrogate markers of LEA in the context of the female athlete triad (Yeager et al. 1993 ; Otis et al. 1997 ) or relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) (Mountjoy et al. 2014 , 2018 , 2023 ) models, whereas the possible influence of physical and psychological stressors on hormonal function are less discussed (Facchinetti et al. 1993 ; Nappi and Facchinetti 2003 ). To our knowledge, references to HC use in research on LEA in athletes (both in the triad and REDs models) are generally limited to reminders that (combined) HC provides exogenous hormones that suppress sex hormone concentrations that are likely to mask menstrual dysfunction, such as the ovulatory disorders (Munro et al. 2022 ), associated with LEA. At present, we are unaware of any literature that specifically discusses the possible influence of progestin‐only HC use on hormonal markers associated with LEA. Where exogenous sex steroids in combined HCs may continue to regulate the HPO axis when faced with LEA and other stressors, how other hormonal axes might respond to LEA and other stressors remains to be elucidated. Given the systemic hormonal changes induced by HCs as well as LEA (and other stressors), it is fair to hypothesize that the exogenous hormones in HCs may have implications for biomarkers used for monitoring athlete health. As such, the purpose of this observational study was to examine data (secondary analysis) from two physique athlete studies carried out at the University of Jyväskylä that was stratified into groups based on HC use (combined HC and progestin‐only HC) and nonuse that is, naturally menstruating females, in order to investigate the possible differences in responses between these groups in terms of changes in selected hormones after planned intentional exposure to LEA induced by diet and physical training. We hypothesized that combined HCs would maintain (already suppressed) concentrations of hormones associated directly with the HPO axis (estradiol and testosterone) during LEA but that combined HC and progestin‐only HC users would experience comparable endocrine changes to participants with natural cycles in hormones not directly regulated by the HPO axis, specifically IGF‐1, cortisol, triiodothyronine, and leptin.

extracted_data.document_summary: This observational study, a secondary analysis, investigated the influence of hormonal contraceptive (HC) use on selected hormonal biomarkers and body composition metrics in 36 female physique athletes exposed to diet and physical training-induced low energy availability (LEA). Over approximately 23 weeks of LEA during competition preparation, estradiol and total testosterone concentrations remained stable in combined HC users but significantly decreased in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females. Serum IGF-1, triiodothyronine (T3), and leptin decreased comparably in all groups, while serum cortisol concentrations remained statistically unchanged. The study concluded that exogenous hormones in combined HCs may maintain already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis function in the presence of LEA, whereas LEA-induced changes in IGF-1, T3, and leptin are comparable across all groups irrespective of HC use. Body composition changes (fat mass, body fat %, VL CSA, body mass, fat-free mass, and energy availability) were also differentially influenced.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by voluntary dietary restriction and concurrent resistance and aerobic training, with an observational comparison across hormonal contraceptive use
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants underwent approximately 23 weeks of planned low energy availability (defined as < 30 kcal 7kg 21 FFM 7day 21) involving voluntary energy restriction and high volumes of resistance training (~5 times/week) and aerobic training (~4 times/week, adjusted pre/post-competition). This was followed by a ~23-week recovery period, totaling ~46 weeks of observation. The study also compared physiological states across three groups (combined HC users, progestin-only HC users, and naturally menstruating females) at pre, post, and recovery time points. During recovery, energy availability differed between groups: progestin-only and naturally menstruating females maintained lower EA (< 30 kcal 7kg 21 FFM 7day 21), while combined HC users had higher EA (> 40 kcal 7kg 21 FFM 7day 21). No dose-response comparisons for LEA intensity or specific hormonal contraceptive dosages were reported, as it was an observational study.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Stable in combined HC users; decreased significantly in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females from pre to post, with some recovery in progestin-only HC users
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In combined HC users, estradiol remained stable from pre to post and recovery, having already been low at baseline due to HPO axis suppression. In progestin-only HC users, it decreased significantly from pre to post (p=0.031) and then increased significantly from post to recovery (p=0.015). In naturally menstruating females, it decreased significantly from pre to post (p=0.006). Overall, there was a significant main effect for time (F=5.543, p=0.024).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary female sex steroid, involved in regulating the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis, reproductive function, bone health, muscle mass, strength, metabolism, and cardiovascular function
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by diet and physical training in female physique athletes, with a comparative analysis across combined hormonal contraceptive users, progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users, and naturally menstruating females at pre, post, and recovery time points
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Maintenance in combined HC users indicates already suppressed HPO axis function by exogenous hormones, potentially masking LEA effects, and could be seen as a negative endocrine consequence. A significant decrease in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females reflects LEA-induced HPO axis suppression, indicating reproductive health status and increased risk of endocrine and menstrual dysfunction, reduced performance, and health issues associated with REDs.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Stable in combined HC users; significantly decreased from pre to post in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females, with some recovery in both groups but remaining lower than pre in naturally menstruating females at recovery
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In combined HC users, total testosterone concentrations showed no significant change over time. In progestin-only HC users, concentrations decreased significantly from pre to post (p=0.005) and then increased significantly from post to recovery (p=0.011). In naturally menstruating females, concentrations decreased significantly from pre to post (p<0.001) and increased significantly from post to recovery (p<0.001), but remained significantly lower than pre at recovery (p=0.043). At post, concentrations were lower in progestin-only HC users (p=0.004) and naturally menstruating females (p<0.001) compared to combined HC users. A significant group*time interaction was observed (F=3.819, p=0.015).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Sex steroid hormone (androgen), influenced by the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis and energy availability, involved in muscle growth, bone density, libido, and energy metabolism in females, and serves as a precursor for estradiol biosynthesis
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by diet and physical training in female physique athletes, with a comparative analysis across combined hormonal contraceptive users, progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users, and naturally menstruating females at pre, post, and recovery time points
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Maintenance in combined HC users suggests suppressed HPO axis function, potentially helping to maintain baseline concentrations despite LEA. A decrease in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females indicates LEA-induced HPO axis suppression, influencing muscle anabolic potential, bone health, and overall vitality. Lower testosterone is associated with LEA and training-related menstrual dysfunction.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Decreased significantly from pre to post in all groups, then increased from post to recovery, with overall lower levels in combined HC users at baseline and recovery compared to naturally menstruating females
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Naturally menstruating females had significantly higher IGF-1 at pre than combined HC users (p=0.002). All groups (combined HC, progestin-only HC, naturally menstruating females) showed significant decreases from pre to post (p=0.007, p<0.001, and p<0.001, respectively) after ~23 weeks of LEA. All groups also showed significant increases from post to recovery (p=0.028, p<0.001, and p<0.001, respectively), with levels comparable to pre-treatment in most cases. At recovery, IGF-1 was significantly higher in progestin-only users (p=0.028) and naturally menstruating females (p=0.002) than combined HC users. A significant group*time interaction was observed (F=3.020, p=0.025).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Insulin-like Growth Factor 1, primarily produced by the liver in response to Growth Hormone (GH), mediating the GH-IGF-1 axis. It is crucial for cell growth, metabolism, tissue repair, muscle protein synthesis, hypertrophy, and inhibition of muscle protein breakdown
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by diet and physical training in female physique athletes (defined as < 30 kcal 7kg 21 FFM 7day 21), with a comparative analysis across combined hormonal contraceptive users, progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users, and naturally menstruating females at pre, post, and recovery time points
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A comparable decrease in all groups indicates negative endocrine consequences of LEA, affecting training adaptations, muscle maintenance, and overall health, potentially due to LEA-induced GH resistance. It serves as an indicator of anabolic status and overall metabolic health, reflecting potential for tissue growth and repair, and can be a biomarker for short-term LEA.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Statistically unchanged over time in all groups, but generally higher in combined HC users compared to other groups
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cortisol concentrations remained statistically unchanged throughout the investigation (pre, post ~23 weeks of LEA, and recovery) in all groups, with no significant main effect for time (F=0.953, p=0.391) or group*time interaction (F=0.654, p=0.626). However, overall, cortisol was significantly higher in combined HC users than in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females (significant main effect for group, F=21.452, p<0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary glucocorticoid stress hormone, regulated by the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. It is involved in regulating metabolism, immune response, inflammation, and maintaining blood pressure, acting as a catabolic hormone
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by diet and physical training in female physique athletes, with a comparative analysis across combined hormonal contraceptive users, progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users, and naturally menstruating females at pre, post, and recovery time points
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Statistically unchanged levels across groups over time suggest maintained HPA axis homeostasis despite LEA, or adaptive mechanisms. However, the generally higher concentrations in combined HC users indicate a differential baseline stress response, which is relevant for metabolic regulation, muscle tissue remodeling, and overall physiological stress.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Decreased significantly from pre to post in all groups. Combined HC users recovered to pre levels, while progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females remained significantly lower at recovery. Overall, T3 was higher in combined HC users
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: All groups (combined HC, progestin-only HC, naturally menstruating females) decreased significantly from pre to post (p<0.001, p<0.008, and p<0.001, respectively) after ~23 weeks of LEA. Combined HC users increased back to pre-treatment concentrations at recovery (p=0.009). Progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females remained significantly lower than pre at recovery (p=0.042 and p<0.001, respectively), despite an increase from post to recovery in naturally menstruating females (p=0.003). Overall, T3 was significantly higher in combined HC users than in progestin-only HC users (p=0.009) and naturally menstruating females (p=0.001). There was a significant main effect for time (F=28.992, p<0.001) and group (F=8.967, p<0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Active thyroid hormone (T3), crucial for regulating metabolic rate, growth, and development across various organ systems, as part of the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid (HPT) axis. It is important for weight management, muscle function, and recovery
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by diet and physical training in female physique athletes (defined as < 30 kcal 7kg 21 FFM 7day 21), with a comparative analysis across combined hormonal contraceptive users, progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users, and naturally menstruating females at pre, post, and recovery time points. Relevant for both short-term and prolonged LEA
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreases indicate negative endocrine consequences of LEA, potentially impacting metabolic rate, energy production, muscle function, and overall physiological well-being, irrespective of HC use. Lower T3 is associated with amenorrhea and suspected long-term LEA, and it is important for weight management and recovery.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Decreased significantly from pre to post in all groups due to LEA; increased significantly from post to recovery in all groups but remained significantly lower at recovery than pre in naturally menstruating females
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: All groups (combined HC, progestin-only HC, naturally menstruating females) showed significant decreases from pre to post (p=0.011, p<0.001, and p<0.001, respectively) after ~23 weeks of LEA. All groups significantly increased from post to recovery (p=0.002, p=0.001, and p=0.001, respectively), with levels generally returning towards baseline. However, leptin concentrations remained significantly lower at recovery than pre in naturally menstruating females (p=0.021), especially those who continued to experience LEA. There was a significant main effect for time (F=24.032, p<0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Adipokine hormone produced by adipocytes, playing a key role in appetite regulation, energy balance, and metabolism by signaling fat stores to the brain. It is upregulated when fat mass or energy balance is positive and downregulated with low energy availability
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Low energy availability (LEA) induced by diet and physical training in female physique athletes, with a comparative analysis across combined hormonal contraceptive users, progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users, and naturally menstruating females at pre, post, and recovery time points
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A comparable decrease in all groups indicates negative endocrine consequences of LEA, signaling chronic energy deficit irrespective of HC use. This downregulation, which can occur even with short-term LEA, negatively affects reproductive, metabolic, and bone health, and is associated with suppression of HPO and HPT axes and activation of the HPA axis. It is an important indicator of fat mass, energy status, and metabolic regulation.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Whole body (derived from body composition analysis)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Decreased from pre to post in all groups. Combined and progestin-only HC users returned to baseline, while naturally menstruating females remained significantly lower at recovery than pre
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Fat mass was significantly higher in naturally menstruating females than progestin-only HC users at pre (p=0.027). All three groups significantly decreased from pre to post (p<0.001). Combined HC users and progestin-only HC users returned to baseline after a significant increase (p<0.001) from post to recovery. Naturally menstruating females had significantly lower fat mass at recovery than pre (p=0.001) despite a significant increase from post to recovery (p<0.001). A significant group*time interaction observed.
